issues.item: Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: These items imply a trauma involving a direct interpersonal assault by a perpetrator with ongoing home-intrusion danger. That is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of witnessed other trauma, where the patient observed trauma happening to someone else rather than being personally harmed.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
issues.explanation: The rest of the profile is broadly coherent for PTSD with strong links among triggers, threat, appraisals, and memory, but these two items specifically shift the narrative to a victim-of-assault formulation rather than a witness formulation.

vignette: Dr. Nguyen had always been a composed man, but that changed the day he witnessed the devastating hospital fire that claimed several lives. The smell of burnt flesh and smoke still lingered in his memory, transporting him back to that fateful moment. Even now, 10 years later, the scent of burnt offerings at the Buddhist temple near his home could trigger an overwhelming sense of dread. On hot summer days, when the temperature on his skin felt similar to that day, he would become irritable and withdrawn. Stress, too, had become a potent trigger - whenever he felt overwhelmed by the demands of his surgical practice or the pressures of family life, memories of the fire would resurface. As a surgeon, Dr. Nguyen was accustomed to being in control, but these triggers made him feel like a passenger on a runaway train. To cope, he began pushing away positive emotions because they felt unsafe - a sense of joy or contentment would inevitably be followed by a plunge into despair. He also tried hard not to think about the trauma, suppressing thoughts and images that lingered in his mind's eye. Watching TV programs or films about similar events was out of the question; even reading about them made him anxious. Despite these efforts, Dr. Nguyen couldn't shake off the feeling of being on high alert. Loud noises would startle him, making him jump in his seat. He found himself taking unnecessary risks, almost as if he needed to prove to himself that he was still in control. The memory of the fire had become a minefield - sometimes it felt like it belonged to someone else, while at other times the emotional intensity would overwhelm him without any clear image or memory. When memories did surface, they were disjointed and confusing, like fragments of a shattered mirror. Dr. Nguyen's body seemed to have developed a mind of its own, reacting as if he was still in danger even when he was safe. He felt defective, as if there was something fundamentally wrong with him as a person. Constant vigilance had become his default state - he had to be especially careful because you never knew what could happen next. These negative appraisals had him convinced that he needed to stay one step ahead of danger at all times. The more Dr. Nguyen struggled to make sense of his memories, the more they seemed to slip through his fingers like sand. His avoidance behaviors were a coping mechanism, but they also made it harder for him to confront the trauma head-on. The maladaptive strategies he employed only reinforced the negative appraisals that had taken hold - that he was flawed and that danger lurked around every corner. As Dr. Nguyen navigated his daily life, these causal connections tightened like a noose. Triggers led to avoidance behaviors, which in turn fueled threat responses, negative appraisals, and distorted memories. The cycle seemed inescapable, yet he knew he needed help. His wife had grown concerned about the toll this was taking on their relationship, and Dr. Nguyen couldn't shake off the feeling that he was losing himself to the trauma. It was this realization that finally brought him to seek therapy - a desperate bid to break free from the cycle of suffering and reclaim his life.
